draft.title: Income and wealth
card: money a person receives over a period of time, such as wages, interest or rent. It is a flow, measured per week, month or year.
the value of what a person owns at a point in time, less what they owe. It can include a home, savings and shares.
Debts reduce wealth. A person who owns a home worth $600,000 and owes $400,000 on a loan has $200,000 of wealth from the home.
Income and wealth are linked but not the same. A person can have a high income and little wealth, or a low income and a lot of wealth.
draft.remember: Income is what you receive over time. Wealth is what you own, less what you owe.

a.q: Which of these is an example of income rather than wealth?
opts: Wages paid to Jess for a week of work
The savings Jess has in her bank account
Jess's share of a mining company
a.why: Wages are money received over a period, so they are income. Savings, shares and a car are things Jess owns at a point in time, so they count towards wealth. Savings can look like income because they are money, but they are a stock owned, not a payment received.
a.clue: Which one is money received over a period of time?

b.q: Ravi owns a flat worth $500,000 and owes $450,000 on his home loan. He owns no other assets. What is Ravi's wealth?
opts: $50,000, the value of the flat less the loan
$500,000, the full value of the flat
b.why: Wealth is what a person owns less what they owe, so $500,000 - $450,000 = $50,000. Counting the full $500,000 ignores the debt, which is the most tempting mistake.
b.clue: Take away what Ravi owes from what he owns.

a.best: Wages paid to Jess for a week of work

b.best: $50,000, the value of the flat less the loan
